questions.question: Distinguish between the site and the situation of a settlement, and explain what wet-point and dry-point sites are.
questions.expected_answer: Site is the actual land a settlement is built on — relief, drainage, soil, water supply, aspect — while situation is the settlement's position relative to its surroundings: other settlements, routes, rivers and resources. A wet-point site is chosen in a dry region because water is available there, such as a Karoo farmstead at a borehole; a dry-point site is chosen in a wet, flood-prone area on higher, drier ground above the floodplain.

questions.question: Explain the difference between dispersed and nucleated rural settlement patterns and give the main reason each develops.
questions.expected_answer: Dispersed settlement scatters individual homesteads far apart, each on its own land — typical of large privately owned commercial farms where the farmer lives on the land worked. Nucleated settlement clusters dwellings tightly around a central point such as a water source, church or kraal, with farmland around the outside — typical of communal land tenure, shared water, defence and community life, as in many villages of the former homelands.

questions.question: Name the four rural village shapes and give the cause that builds each one.
questions.expected_answer: Round — dwellings in a circle around a central open space or cattle kraal, built for protection and community life. Linear — dwellings stretched in a line along a road, river or canal because each wants frontage on the routeway. T-shaped — buildings along both arms where a side road meets a main road, drawn by passing trade at the junction. Crossroad — buildings along all four arms where two roads cross, for the same junction-trade reason.
